'''Vida Mary Stout''' (20 February 1930 – 21 July 2012) was a New Zealand [[limnographer]] and academic administrator.<ref name="rsnzobit">{{cite web|title=Obituary|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170806100802/http://rsnzbranch.org.nz/prominent.htm|archive-date=6 Aug 2017 |url=http://rsnzbranch.org.nz/prominent.htm|website=Royal Society of New Zealand, Canterbury Branch|access-date=6 August 2017}}</ref> She was the first woman to be [[Dean (education)|Dean of Science]] at a New Zealand university.<ref>{{Cite news|title=No slowing down for retiring ecologist|last=Meduna|first=Veronika|date=26 March 1996|work=The Press (Christchurch)}}</ref>

==Biography==
Stout was the daughter of [[Thomas Duncan MacGregor Stout]] and granddaughter of [[Robert Stout]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stamplink.com/genealogy/pearce/d1286.htm |title=Seventh Generation |publisher=Stamplink.com |access-date=2012-09-23}}</ref> Born and raised in [[Wellington]], Stout was educated at [[Woodford House]] in Hawke's Bay, where she was Dux.<ref name="nzfssobit">{{cite web|title=A tribute to Vida Stout|url=http://freshwater.science.org.nz/index.php/about/honorary-past-members/a-tribute-to-vida-stout/|website=New Zealand Freshwater Science Society|access-date=6 August 2017|archive-date=29 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929155532/http://freshwater.science.org.nz/index.php/about/honorary-past-members/a-tribute-to-vida-stout/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

She then studied at [[Victoria University of Wellington|Victoria University College]], where she completed a Bachelor of Science and Masters of Science in zoology. Her Masters thesis was on "[[Wikispecies:Hydracarina|Hydracarina]] from the Wellington province". Stout then completed a PhD at [[Bedford College, University of London]], where she studied [[Daphnia]].<ref name="nzfssobit" />

She returned to New Zealand after post-doctoral work in Sweden and in 1968 she and [[Ann Chapman (freshwater scientist)|Ann Chapman]] founded the New Zealand Limnological Society (now the [[New Zealand Freshwater Sciences Society]]).<ref name="nzfssobit" /> Stout was the first president of the society and later was made an honorary life member.<ref name="nzfssobit" /> She was also a long-term member of the Canterbury branch of the [[Royal Society Te Apārangi|Royal Society of New Zealand]], and was the branch president in 1983.<ref name="rsnzobit" />

Stout was appointed to the Zoology Department at the [[University of Canterbury]] in 1958, where she remained until her retirement in 1996.<ref name="nzfssobit" /> During her tenure she held the positions of dean of science from 1984 to 1998, deputy chair of the university's Academic Administration Committee from 1992 to 1995 and played a role in establishing the Masters in Environmental Science Course.<ref name="nzfssobit" /><ref name="rsnzobit" /> Her research focused on the biology and chemistry of South Island lakes, including the nature and changes in [[zooplankton]] communities over time. She undertook long-term studies on lakes Pearson and [[Lake Grassmere|Grassmere]], near the university's [[Cass, New Zealand|Cass]] field station.<ref name="nzfssobit" />

The University of Canterbury also holds her archives.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://kohika.canterbury.ac.nz/opac_canterbury/scripts/mwimain.dll/144/Description/Web_desc_det_rep?sessionsearch&fld=SISN&exp=141949 |title=Vida Stout: University and course notes |work=digital-library.canterbury.ac.nz |year=2012 |access-date=1 August 2012}}</ref>

After retiring in 1996, Stout continued to go to her office almost every day until the university forbid her access, citing fears for her safety due to her progressive [[Parkinson's disease]], which caused her death in 2012.<ref name="rsnzobit" />

In 2017, Stout was selected as one of the Royal Society Te Apārangi's "[[150 women in 150 words]]", celebrating the contributions of women to knowledge in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Vida Stout|url=https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/150th-anniversary/150-women-in-150-words/1968-2017/new-rsnz-content-7/|access-date=2021-05-11|website=Royal Society Te Apārangi}}</ref>
